title: Scaling model pools & queueing theory deep dive with Orion Research
customer_attendees: Dr. Aaron Cole (Head of ML Infra)
summary: Deep technical discussion about autoscaling strategies for model pools, burst policies and queueing models, tradeoffs between reserved GPUs and burst capacity, KV cache priming and quantization impacts on throughput. Agreed next steps to run a focused benchmark and share cost/latency spreadsheet.
transcript:
Meeting Header: 2025-05-06 16:00 UTC | Duration: 01:18:00 | Attendees: Maya, Liam, Sofia (Redwood) — Aaron, Priya, Ben, Mara (Orion)

[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick goal for today is to walk through how we think about scaling model pools and the queueing behavior when you have mixed traffic — steady-state vs occasional spikes. also call out any on-prem constraints you have.
[00:00:22] Dr. Aaron (Orion): Cool, thanks. we currently run a mix of real-time chat and nightly batch scoring. our latency SLO on chat is 200ms p95, but costs are killing us; we want to understand if dedicated reserved gpus or a burst pool is better.
[00:00:45] Liam (Redwood): got it. at a high level we see two levers — capacity reservation (reserved GPU pools) and elastic burst. reservation gives predictable throughput, no cold starts for KV cache, but has higher baseline cost. burst lets you keep lower committed capacity, but you need a queuing model and pre-warm policies.
[00:01:15] Priya (Orion): can you expand on the queuing model you recommend? we've been thinking in terms of a simple FIFO queue but worried about head-of-line blocking with long generation requests.
[00:01:30] Liam (Redwood): yeah so we model it similar to an M/M/c queue with priority tiers. chat requests go into high-priority lane — small seq len, small token output — while long-form generations go to a separate pool or are throttled. a couple notes: we track token-rate arrival distribution and use that for kernel selection and batching windows.
[00:02:05] Ben (Orion): when you say batching windows, what are we looking at for latency? like do we add 10-40ms to hit token batching efficiency?
[00:02:20] Liam (Redwood): typical additional wait is 5-50ms depending on target batch size. for small latency SLOs we do micro-batching and aggressive prefix caching (KV cache) so we amortize per-token kernel overhead. the tradeoff is throughput/cost — larger batches reduce cost per token.
[00:02:50] Maya (Redwood): and to avoid head-of-line we implement per-priority queues and a concurrency cap per model variant so long-form jobs can't starve the low-latency lane. also we can route to a quantized variant for low-cost fallbacks.
[00:03:20] Dr. Aaron (Orion): how predictable is KV cache warm-up? we saw cold responses when traffic dipped overnight.
[00:03:35] Sofia (Redwood): cold starts are the usual issue — KV cache priming depends on conversation prefixes and model state. options: keep a small warm pool pinned, do background priming tasks that replay hot prefixes, or persist KV snapshots for very common prompts. persistence is space-heavy but gives near-instant hits.
[00:04:05] Priya (Orion): do you have numbers on the cost tradeoff for keeping pinned small pool vs full reservation?
[00:04:20] Liam (Redwood): ballpark: a small pinned pool sized for the p50 concurrent chats (plus some buffer) often costs a fraction of full reservation. e.g., for 10k monthly active users with bursty traffic we saw pinned pool at 20% of the full reserved cost but with 90% similar latency SLAs. will share the deck/spreadsheet.
[00:04:50] [00:04:50] Ben (Orion): any recommendations on quantization for our mix? we use Llama-ish models and are worried about quality regressions.
[00:05:05] Liam (Redwood): we recommend mixed strategy: int8 or awq for short completions and for some reranking/semantics tasks keep fp16. Redwood Optimize can suggest per-route quantization based on eval sets. quality regressions are model and prompt specific — you should run a small eval harness.
[00:05:30] Maya (Redwood): also note that quantization reduces memory footprint which lets you pack more model replicas per GPU and increases concurrency — helps with burst capacity. but there is a warm-up/compile time when switching kernels.
[00:05:55] [00:05:55] Dr. Aaron (Orion): about burst policies: if we set a burst queue, how do we protect against queue spirals where backlog keeps growing?
[00:06:10] Liam (Redwood): two tactics: exponential backoff + admission control, and SLA-aware throttling where we drop or reroute lower-priority requests when queue length/p99 latency crosses thresholds. also have a circuit-breaker fallback to a smaller quantized model or cached response.
[00:06:35] Maya (Redwood): plus auto-scaling rules that consider queue length, token-train arrival rate, and KV-hit rate. we often use a composite metric: scale when moving average of queue length * avg tokens > threshold for 30s.
[00:07:00] Priya (Orion): what about startup time for a new replica? how long until it's ready to serve?
[00:07:15] Sofia (Redwood): depends on model and quantization: warm boot for a full fp16 model might be 40-120s due to weight loading and compilation; quantized int8 can be faster but still tens of seconds. that's why pre-warming with pinned pool or keeping a small standby matters.
[00:07:45] Ben (Orion): is there a recommended ratio reserved vs burst? like commit 50% base, 50% burst?
[00:07:58] Liam (Redwood): empirical rule: size reserved to cover baseline predictable traffic (p50-p75) + safety buffer for KV hit degradation. then allow burst for p95-p99. often 30-70% reserved depending on SLA tolerance. we can run a workload trace analysis to recommend a number.
[00:08:25] [00:08:25] Mara (Orion): we have strict networking constraints — we need VPC/on-prem and KMS integration. will that affect autoscaling?
[00:08:40] Maya (Redwood): the private deployments require some work for bursting because cross-VPC capacity ramping is slower; on-prem autoscaling depends on capacity in your cluster. our private plane supports autoscale within the VPC; cross-region bursts require pre-approved peering. KMS integration for key wrapping doesn't affect scaling much but increases boot validation by a few seconds.
[00:09:10] Priya (Orion): what about queueing algorithm details — do you implement token-aware scheduling?
[00:09:25] Liam (Redwood): yes, token-aware scheduling sorts by estimated remaining tokens so short jobs complete quickly (shortest-job-first heuristic). we combine with weighted priority and per-route concurrency limits. that gives better p95 for chat while maintaining throughput for longer runs.
[00:09:55] [00:09:55] Ben (Orion): curious about cost model — do you charge for reserved GPUs differently?
[00:10:10] Maya (Redwood): reserved capacity contracts have a monthly fee/commit and lower per-token rate. burst usage on top is billed at a premium. we can show modeled invoices for your workload.
[00:10:30] Dr. Aaron (Orion): okay good. let's talk bench specifics — can we run a 48-hour trace replay to see tail behavior?
[00:10:45] Liam (Redwood): yep we can do a trace replay if you can share traffic logs (anonymized). we'll run both open-loop (rate-limited) and closed-loop (feedback) tests, vary model variants (fp16, int8, awq), and include KV warm/cold scenarios.
[00:11:10] Maya (Redwood): for the bench we need: representative logs, a list of hot prefixes, success criteria (p95 latency target, cost per 1k tokens). we'll prepare a test plan and attach to Slack.
[00:11:30] [00:11:30] Priya (Orion): are there any recommended autoscale cool-down windows? we've seen oscillation previously.
[00:11:45] Liam (Redwood): yes set asymmetric cool-downs: scale-up fast (short window) but scale-down slower with hysteresis. use composite scaling triggers (queue length and sustained CPU/GPU utilization) to avoid thrash.
[00:12:05] Ben (Orion): about KV snapshots — how do you manage snapshot size and restore time?
[00:12:20] Sofia (Redwood): snapshot size depends on average prefix length; you can limit snapshot depth to reduce size. restore is typically tens of ms to seconds depending on size; the cost is storage and restore time. for heavy chat workloads we keep shallow snapshots and rely on background priming.
[00:12:45] [00:12:45] Dr. Aaron (Orion): can you do per-tenant reservations? we have multiple internal teams that want isolation.
[00:13:00] Maya (Redwood): yes we support per-tenant pools, separate quotas and RBAC. reserved pools can be dedicated per-tenant or shared with soft reservations.
[00:13:15] Priya (Orion): if we do dedicated per-team pools, how does that impact overall efficiency?
[00:13:30] Liam (Redwood): it reduces statistical multiplexing and may raise cost; recommendation: use shared pool with logical reservations and throttles, unless regulatory needs require physical isolation.
[00:13:55] [00:13:55] Ben (Orion): any pitfalls in private on-prem installs for autoscale?
[00:14:10] Sofia (Redwood): autoscale on-prem requires capacity headroom and a control plane that can trigger provisioning — if you're air-gapped you need pre-provisioned standby or tight integration with your orchestration system. networking and image distribution are common friction points.
[00:14:35] Dr. Aaron (Orion): one more: latency SLOs with multi-model routing (route to smaller model fallback) — how often do you see quality hits?
[00:14:50] Liam (Redwood): it depends on task. for intent detection or classification fallbacks to a distilled model are usually fine. for freeform generation you may see quality delta; use A/B rollouts and evaluate by route to set acceptable thresholds.
[00:15:10] [00:15:10] (discussion continues with specific numbers and examples)
[00:30:00] Liam (Redwood): ok here's a rough worked example — assume 100 qps of chat with average 40 tokens output: token arrival 4k tokens/sec. with fp16 runtime and batching we achieve ~1200 tokens/sec per GPU under typical kernel. if your p95 needs are tight we recommend reserving X GPUs to keep p95 under 200ms; else use 2-3x lower reserved plus burst.
[00:30:40] Priya (Orion): can you share the spreadsheet?
[00:30:45] Maya (Redwood): yes will share modeling sheet and a cost sensitivity toggles.
[00:31:05] [00:31:05] Priya (Orion): regarding tooling, can we get tracing hooks into our console? we want token-level traces.
[00:31:20] Sofia (Redwood): yes Redwood Console exposes token-level cost/latency breakdown per route, and you can add tracing hooks to your logs; we can set retention and access controls.
[00:31:40] Ben (Orion): interesting. for the bench what are the deliverables?
[00:31:55] Maya (Redwood): a bench report with latency distributions, cost per 1k tokens, recommendations for reserved vs burst sizing, suggested autoscale rules and a rollout plan.
[00:32:10] [00:32:10] (discussion about schedule and data sharing)
[00:45:00] Dr. Aaron (Orion): security checklist — SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs — we've got internal auditors.
[00:45:18] Maya (Redwood): Redwood supports SSO/SAML, KMS integrations, per-request audit logs in private deployments, and SOC2. we'll send the security pack. note on KMS: key unwrap adds minimal latency on init, not per-token.
[00:45:40] Priya (Orion): anything else re: networking?
[00:45:50] Sofia (Redwood): we usually recommend peering and dedicated subnets for low-latency private links; packet loss is the silent killer for tail latency.
[00:46:10] [00:46:10] Ben (Orion): final question: how do we monitor for cache miss/priming regressions?
[00:46:25] Liam (Redwood): we instrument KV hit-rate, warm-up duration, and per-prefix cold penalties; set alerts on sudden drops in hit-rate or p99 token latency.
[00:46:45] Maya (Redwood): recap — run a 48h trace replay, share logs and hot prefixes, Redwood to run bench across fp16/int8/awq, provide sizing recommendation and cost model, security pack and test plan.
[00:47:10] Mara (Orion): sounds good, let's do it.
[00:47:20] Priya (Orion): we'll get the logs to you by next Tue.
[00:47:30] [00:47:30] (meeting wraps, some small bits of crosstalk and signoffs)
